Q: Requesting an opinion about an extreme optimization pipeline for a YOLOv8 model A:

Your pipeline is actually well thought out and covers all the right areas compression, distillation, pruning, and quantization are exactly the techniques used in production-grade model optimization. Here is honest feedback on each step:

What is solid:

Adding a P2 head is a legitimate and commonly used trick for small object detection. It taps into higher resolution feature maps (160x160) that the standard P3/P4/P5 heads miss. This is a real improvement, not just theoretical.

Knowledge distillation from YOLOv8m to YOLOv8n using a convex combination loss is exactly how distillation is done in practice. Your formula (Final_Loss = Teacher_Loss * alpha + Ground_Truth_Loss * (1 - alpha)) is correct. Alpha around 0.5-0.7 usually works well as a starting point.

Iterative pruning followed by fine-tuning is the right approach. One-shot pruning tends to destroy accuracy. Your cycle of prune -> fine-tune -> repeat until recovery fails is the standard method used in papers like LeCun's Optimal Brain Damage.

QAT (INT8) at the end is the correct order. Always do quantization last, after the architecture and weights are finalized.

Challenges and things to watch out for:

1. Weight transfer compatibility when you add the P2 head, the backbone weights transfer fine, but the new P2 head layers will be randomly initialized. During step 4 (fine-tuning), the randomly initialized P2 head can produce large gradients early on that destabilize the already-trained backbone. Consider using a lower learning rate for the backbone layers and a higher one for the P2 head initially.

2. Temporal and spatial consistency loss this is harder to implement correctly than it sounds. You need consecutive frames or at least paired samples to compute temporal consistency. If your dataset does not have video sequences or frame ordering, this loss cannot be computed meaningfully.

3. Distillation before pruning make sure you are distilling into YOLOv8n first, then pruning the distilled YOLOv8n. If you prune first then distill, the student model has fewer parameters to absorb the teacher knowledge, which usually gives worse results.

4. QAT after pruning can compound accuracy loss each step (pruning, quantization) costs some accuracy. If your pruned model is already near the accuracy floor, INT8 quantization might push it below acceptable thresholds. Always benchmark accuracy after each step, not just at the end.

Overall verdict: the pipeline is sound and implementable. The complexity is high, so I would suggest validating each step independently on a small dataset before running the full pipeline end to end. That way you can isolate which step is causing issues if accuracy drops unexpectedly.

Q: How to get the next word after a keyword A:

Your pattern is a logical choice, but note that a hyphen is not included in the \w range of characters. Also, preg_split() is not the most convenient tool for this job - preg_match_all() is advisable. To improve pattern performance avoid using a lookbehind.

Compare the step count of the lookbehind pattern in Giacomo1968's answer on their provided string versus a full string match reset pattern without any lookarounds.

input: This is a string, keyword next, some more text. keyword next-word. keyword another_word. Okay, keyword do-rae-mi-fa_so_la.

pattern matches steps
#(?<=\bkeyword\s)[\w-]+# 4 181
#\bkeyword\s\K[\w-]+# 4 49

With the lookbehind pattern, the regex engine must stop and check the lookbehind expression every time a sequence of one or more word or hyphen characters is encountered in the string. This costs more steps and slows the performance.

With the full string match reset, the engine never has to stop and look backward; it qualifies substrings by traversing the string normally from left to right.

\K is quite handy in PHP regex patterns because it allows matching a substring then "forgetting" that substring so that the next matched characters are isolated as the full string match. PHP Demo

$string = 'This is a string, keyword next, some more text. keyword next-word. keyword another_word. Okay, keyword do-rae-mi-fa_so_la.';

preg_match_all('#\bkeyword\s\K[\w-]+#', $string, $m);
var_export($m);

Output:

array (
  0 => 
  array (
    0 => 'next',
    1 => 'next-word',
    2 => 'another_word',
    3 => 'do-rae-mi-fa_so_la',
  ),
)

For topical completeness, preg_split() can be used and it provides a simpler result structure versus preg_match_all(). I probably wouldn't use this in a project because I find the pattern less intuitive than the above regex, but I'll demonstrate for academic reasons. PHP Demo

var_export(
    preg_split(
        '/.*?(?:\bkeyword ([\w-]+))?/',
        $string,
        0,
        PREG_SPLIT_NO_EMPTY  | PREG_SPLIT_DELIM_CAPTURE
    )
);

Output:

array (
  0 => 'next',
  1 => 'next-word',
  2 => 'another_word',
  3 => 'do-rae-mi-fa_so_la',
)

This lazily consumes the beginning of the string until a potentially non-existent match is found, then captures the subsequent word. This effectively splits the string on everything that is not desired in the result array.

Q: Visual Studio 2022 - Fortran - Debugging Issue A:

I am using VS2022 with OneAPI 2025.3.0. My SLN is built by CMake and includes DLLs from Fortran, C and C++ code. The project has several hundred subroutines, 98% in Fortran. I have a similar problem that may be relevant, trying to watch more complex variables in Fortran. I can watch arrays and simple variables (integers, reals, etc.) with Watch and Local windows but cannot watch variables like matrices or other more complex structures. The only workaround I have found is this: I put the variable into its own common block where it is the only member:

      REAL POTCONS(3,3)
      COMMON /POTCOM/ POTCONS

Then when I'm running and single-stepping I can see the variable POTCONS when I put this in the Watch window.

      (float(*)[3][3])POTCOM

So I'm using C-language syntax to point to the one-variable POTCOM common block, and it lets me inspect (and change) the content, though it is 0-indexed and row/column reversed. This workaround is so lame. It seems like a problem that Microsoft and Intel could figure out. Years ago I (paid for and) owned VS2010 with Intel Visual Fortran 2011, and never had a problem with watching any kind of variable in the same code base. The problem seems to be isolated in the Fortran. I have no problem with C++ watches of complicated variables.

The option to unset "Load debug symbols in external process (Native only)" did not solve the issue for me.

Suggestions are always welcome.

Q: Confused about C++ linkage A:

what happens when you link a static library to another static library?

You don't. Static libraries are not linked. They are akin to .zip files, just a loose collection of object files (.obj on Windows). You can use librarian tool (lib.exe on Windows) to extract .obj files from and combine them into .lib files; but that's not really linking (in that it doesn't at all look at symbols provided or required by those .obj files).

Linking occurs when you build a "module" - on Windows, either an .exe (executable) or a .dll (dynamic link library aka shared library). At that point, you have to provide to the linker all the .obj and .lib files necessary to satisfy all mutual dependencies.

I know MSBuild provides a the /MT /MD and /LLD switches

/MT, /MD and /LD are options to the C++ compiler. To the extent MSBuild takes them, it just passes them along when invoking the compiler. These switches determine how the code is generated in an .obj file produced by the compiler (using different flavors of the C++ runtime library requires different generated code). That .obj file can be later used as an input to the linker, either directly or indirectly via a static library, to build an .EXE or a .DLL. It's only required that all .obj files that go into linking a module were built with the same runtime option.

about the "classical model" of linking

Yes, that's mostly how linking works, at least to the first approximation. (There are options like link-time code generation and whole-program optimization that complicate matters.)

Re: POD and extern "C" and explicit import/export.

You are conflating two different issues. Using PODs and extern "C" in the shared library's interface is done to have a stable ABI (application binary interface). The binary layout of non-POD types, and the name mangling convention for non-C functions, are not standardized; so if you build a DLL using such types and functions, it could only reliably be used by an EXE built with the same version of the same compiler with the same settings. Which kinda defeats the purpose of a DLL.

Explicit export/import (using __declspec(dllexport) / __declspec(dllimport) or via .DEF files) is specific to how Windows DLLs work. Shared libraries on Linux-like systems don't require that, and work more like static libraries (pretty much every function and global variable is automatically externally visible).

On Windows, when you link a DLL, the linker also produces an export library (a file with .LIB extension, just like a static library; but the export library doesn't contain object code, only the metadata on what symbols are available from the companion DLL). You can pass that .LIB file to the linker when building another DLL or EXE, and it would embded the metadata into the module to help the OS loader automatically locate and load the original DLL and patch in the addresses of its exported functions. You use this mechanism all the time even if you might not realize it - every Windows API function comes from some OS-provided DLL (e.g. CreateWindow is implemented in user32.dll, and you link with user32.lib export library to resolve this dependency).

(I'm vague on show shared libraries work on Linux-like systems; I'm a Windows guy myself.)

Q: Pytorch engine saves the batch size : how do I save the model in a way allowing me to input one image at a time? A: 
The error RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied is happening because your model's first nn.Linear layer expects a batched input of shape [batch_size, 32*29*29], but when you pass a single image, testTensor has shape [3, 256, 256] — missing the batch dimension entirely.

The model itself is fine you just need to add one line before inference.

Looking at your loading code, the fix goes right before you call the model:

    loadedModel = myCNN().to(device)
    loadedModel.load_state_dict(torch.load("your_checkpoint.pth"))
    loadedModel.eval()

    testImage = "/content/Mario and Luigi ..."
    testTensor = decode_image(testImage).float()

    testTransforms = Transforms.Compose([
        Transforms.Resize((256, 256))
    ])
    testTensor = testTransforms(testTensor)

    # ADD THIS LINE — gives shape [1, 3, 256, 256] instead of [3, 256, 256]
    testTensor = testTensor.unsqueeze(0).to(device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        output = loadedModel(testTensor)
        predicted_class = output.argmax(dim=1)
        print(predicted_class)

The batch size is never saved in the model weights ModelCheckpoint only saves the parameters. The model just always needs that first dimension, even when it's 1.

Two extra things worth fixing in your code:

- Move model.eval() outside the torch.no_grad() block — it is a mode switch, not an inference step
- Always move your tensor to the same device as the model with .to(device), otherwise you will get a device mismatch error
